title: Presidential vs Parliamentary
hook: Two democracies can run on totally different wiring: in one, voters pick the leader directly; in the other, the legislature does — and that changes everything downstream.
key_points: Presidential systems separately elect the executive, who is independent of the legislature.
Parliamentary systems pick the executive (prime minister) from within the legislature.
A prime minister governs only while holding the legislature's confidence; a president has a fixed term.
The trade-off: presidential systems offer stability and clear separation; parliamentary ones, flexibility and easier removal.
content_html: Among democracies, one of the deepest structural divides is how the executive relates to the legislature. In a presidential system, the two are elected separately and stand on their own foundations: voters choose a president directly (or nearly so) for a fixed term, and that president is not a member of the legislature and cannot be dismissed by it for ordinary political disagreement. In a parliamentary system, the wiring is fused: voters elect the legislature, and the executive — a prime minister and cabinet — is drawn from within it and governs only as long as it retains the legislature's support.
extra_html: That single difference cascades. A prime minister who loses a vote of no confidence must usually resign or call an election, making the executive continuously accountable and relatively easy to replace; a president with a fixed term is harder to remove, typically only through an exceptional process like impeachment. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the familiar trade-off this creates. Presidential systems offer stability and a clear separation of powers, but a president and a hostile legislature can deadlock, and a failing leader is hard to dislodge. Parliamentary systems offer flexibility — a government can be reshuffled or replaced without a national crisis — but can suffer instability when no party commands a reliable majority. Many countries adopt hybrids (semi-presidential systems) that blend a directly elected president with a prime minister answerable to parliament.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: The Executive
related.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

related.title: The Legislature
related.hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

flashcards.prompt: What's the core difference between presidential and parliamentary systems?
flashcards.back_html: In a presidential system the executive is separately elected and independent of the legislature; in a parliamentary system the executive is drawn from, and answerable to, the legislature.

flashcards.prompt: How can a prime minister typically be removed mid-term that a president usually cannot?

choices.text: By losing the legislature's confidence (a no-confidence vote)
By a direct public recall election held every month
By the head of state alone, for any reason

flashcards.explanation_html: A prime minister governs only while commanding the legislature's confidence; a president generally serves a fixed term, removable only by exceptional means.

flashcards.prompt: What is a commonly cited trade-off between the two systems?

choices.text: Presidential offers fixed-term stability and clear separation; parliamentary offers flexibility and easier removal
Presidential systems have no legislature at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Fixed terms give stability but can entrench a failing leader; fused power lets parliaments replace a government quickly but can be less stable.
